title: Kurt Gödel: the Königsberg abstract of 1930, Über die Vollständigkeit des Logikkalküls
edition: K. Gödel, „Über die Vollständigkeit des Logikkalküls“, abstract of the lecture of 6 September 1930 at the Tagung für exakte Erkenntnislehre, Königsberg, in the report of the 91st Versammlung Deutscher Naturforscher und Ärzte, Die Naturwissenschaften 18, Heft 47–49 (28 November 1930), p. 1068 — the Archive's microfilm issue sim_naturwissenschaften_1930-11-28_18_47-49, OCR layer. The same issue carries David Hilbert's Königsberg address „Naturerkennen und Logik“ (pp. 959–963), which closes „Wir müssen wissen, Wir werden wissen.“, and the abstracts of Carnap, Heyting and the other speakers of the Tagung

scope: Held: Gödel's own abstract of the completeness theorem, as printed in the Naturwissenschaften report of the Königsberg meeting, in the issue that first carried it. The OCR reads the title's last word as „Logikkalkiils“; the loci avoid it. Not held: the completeness paper itself, „Die Vollständigkeit der Axiome des logischen Funktionenkalküls“, Monatshefte für Mathematik und Physik 37 (1930), 349–360. It is in the public domain in the United States, but no copy could be reached: the Internet Archive holds the Monatshefte for vol. 36 (1929, bwb_C0-AYK-298) and none for vol. 37; HathiTrust holds Cornell's vol. 36–37 in full view (coo.31924000966790) and refused the seating's requests on 2026-10-30 with a Cloudflare challenge and a block page. The announcement of the incompleteness results, „Einige metamathematische Resultate über Entscheidungsdefinitheit und Widerspruchsfreiheit“, Anzeiger der Akademie der Wissenschaften in Wien 67 (1930), 214–215, is also public domain in the United States and was not found on the Archive. The incompleteness paper of 1931 is not seated: it opens in the United States on 2027-01-01. The Königsberg discussion (Erkenntnis 2, 1931) opens on the same date.

why_seated: The completeness theorem was first told to the public in a paragraph of a congress report, beside the address in which Hilbert answered the ignorabimus with „Wir müssen wissen, Wir werden wissen.“ The seat holds that page in the issue that carried both. The paper of 1931 that unsettled Hilbert's answer waits for its term to end.
